extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in patent NLP, patent analytics, and automated patent examination (including patent examiners, patent data scientists, and IP policy researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and evaluates criteria, methods, and metrics for multiple patent-related NLP tasks (information extraction, novelty/inventiveness prediction, patentability/granting/litigation prediction, valuation, forecasting, and innovation recommendation). Aimed at guiding research and system design for automated patent analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-based information extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-defined rules can lead to precise extraction so that this process is transparent and interpretable (e.g., rules like ‘The term user followed by can and adverbs, such as readily efficiently, quickly and easily’ to extract affordances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: precise, transparent, interpretable. Cons: creating and maintaining rules is time-consuming, difficult, and biased; rule-based methods may struggle with variability and complexity of natural language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep-learning-based information extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep learning methods require labeled datasets that include entities or relations for training and use architectures such as LSTM or transformers (e.g., T5 for long descriptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: handle wide variety of expressions, scalable with data and compute, capture complex patterns. Cons: require large high-quality annotated data and computational resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patent descriptions vs claims/abstracts for IE
rubrics_metrics.description: Most research focuses on claims and abstracts, neglecting description parts that contain essential technical information because descriptions are notably longer and require models that can load long text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should consider frameworks (e.g., T5-based) capable of processing long descriptions to leverage essential technical information in descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal definition of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is novel if there is no older document or disclosure that alone includes and/or describes all essential features of the invention. Novelty can also hold if aggregation of prior disclosures does not reveal all essential features or experts would not find it obvious to integrate missing features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty assessment critically relies on the concept of features (those elements outlined in the patent claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Features as basis for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Features are the elements the invention needs to comprise to be the invention and are outlined in the patent claims (independent claims list essential features). Features can be physical elements, properties, or processing steps; in many jurisdictions features cannot be negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature identification must handle synonymy and homonyms; features cannot generally be introduced as negative limitations after filing; later exclusions are limited by the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish patent novelty vs technological originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent novelty (legal sense) is assessed based on prior art and disclosures, whereas technological novelty/originality is analyzed in a technical context focusing on the advancement and uniqueness of the technological contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should explicitly differentiate these concepts when designing models or indicators because methods optimizing for technological originality may not satisfy legal novelty criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty prediction task definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty and inventiveness prediction is typically cast as a binary classification task: determine whether a new patent is novel given the existing patent database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This automated system is intended as an auxiliary tool for novelty examination to improve quality and efficiency; task framing can also be extended to assess degrees of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator-based methods for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pre-defined indicators (e.g., citations, classification codes, proximity measures) to measure patent novelty compared to prior art; examples include Verhoeven et al.'s three dimensions (novelty in recombination, technological origins, scientific origins) and Plantec et al.'s proximity indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators are scored/weighted to compute novelty scores. Limitations: selection and weighting of indicators can be subjective and may not capture nuanced legal aspects of invention features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlier-detection approach for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumes novel inventions are outliers in the patent landscape; represent patents via embeddings (Word2Vec, Doc2Vec, LSA) and apply outlier algorithms (e.g., Local Outlier Factor) to flag novel patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations: does not align strictly with legal novelty (feature-based comparison); may flag statistically unusual but not legally novel patents; embedding differences may not reflect feature differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity-measurements for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute similarity (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) between target patent and existing patents using text representations (embeddings, keyword vectors); patents with low similarity considered more novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using titles/abstracts or generic text representations can fail to assess legal novelty because they may not disclose essential features; high-dimensional keyword vectors or embeddings may correlate with technological novelty but not legal novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervised learning for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Train classifiers (SVM, Naive Bayes, neural networks, LSTM, GRU, BERT-based) using target claims and relevant prior art to predict novelty; inputs often include target claims and cited prior-art paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns: deep models can be black-box and may not detect novelty via explicit feature comparison. Explainable approaches (e.g., BERT models that output relevant claim sets) can provide supporting evidence and improve trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability assessment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability generally requires novelty, inventiveness/non-obviousness (sufficient inventive step beyond prior art), and utility (usefulness/practical application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability assessment is more comprehensive and challenging than novelty prediction alone and often requires combining novelty and non-obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability via feature-combination comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose patent claims into features and formulate feature combinations; compare the target patent feature combination with prior art to evaluate novelty and non-obviousness following legal definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof-of-concept methods exist but may not scale; limitations include inability to detect homonyms/synonyms; recent LLMs may help improve feature extraction and matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granting prediction task definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Predict whether a patent application will be granted or terminally rejected by examiners (i.e., granting prediction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such prediction can aid examiners, applicants, and investors; datasets and model performance vary, and reported accuracies have been modest, indicating substantial room for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granting prediction methodology: text and metadata fusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine patent text (abstracts and claims) and metadata (filing info, citations, network attributes) using text encoders (LSTM/CNN/BERT) and network embeddings (ActiveHNE) with attention mechanisms to predict grant outcomes (e.g., PARCEL framework).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining modalities (text + metadata) tends to improve accuracy versus text-only methods; dataset heterogeneity complicates direct comparisons across studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation prediction inputs and importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Predict whether a patent will cause litigation using multiple inputs: metadata (number of claims, patent type), claim texts, citation-graph features summarizing patent citations, and lawsuit records of companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings show metadata has the highest impact on litigation prediction; including lawsuit records and improved representations of patent-company relations can increase precision significantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent valuation task definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the monetary or strategic value of a single patent, application, or portfolio; the value depends on portfolio context, functionality, scope of claims, dependencies on other patents, and potential for licensing or blocking competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuation can be formulated as regression (predict numeric value) or classification (high-quality vs not, multi-level quality grading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent valuation indicators and dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pre-defined indicators and dimensions (e.g., Hu et al.'s four dimensions: legal value, technological value, competitiveness value, scientific value) and observable proxies (citations, assigned revenue share, licensing fees, patent sales) to evaluate patent quality/value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations correlate with value but have large variability and lag; direct economic indicators (revenue shares, licensing fees) may be more accurate where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text and network features for valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract semantic/textual features (attention-based CNNs, bidirectional LSTM) from patent texts and combine with graph/network representations (GNNs, citation networks) to predict patent quality/value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multimodal approaches combining text and network features outperform single-modality baselines in many experiments; multi-task learning (e.g., jointly predicting high-value and standard-essential patents) can yield modest improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emerging technology forecasting
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary classification task predicting whether a patent contains emerging technologies, often identified by clustering signals or patent indicators (patent class, number of citations) and sometimes augmented by web/social measures of impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods include supervised models, labeling via external frameworks (e.g., Gartner hype cycles), GANs to augment scarce positive samples, and multi-source datasets (patents + web articles); reported precision varies (~70–77%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology life cycle prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Predict the stage of a technology (introduction, growth, maturity, saturation) using patent-derived indicators (patent class, citations) and models such as Hidden Markov Models that learn state transition probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic patent indicators alone may be insufficient; combining extrinsic factors (market trends, social adoption, competition) is recommended for more accurate life-cycle prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent application trend prediction (company-level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Predict patent classification codes a company will apply for in the future given the sequence of its past filings (company-dependent forecasting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dynamic graph representation learning methods have been used; recall remains low in reported experiments, indicating significant room for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation recommendation by concept association analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify key concepts within patent documents and analyze their associations to discover novel combinations of concepts and suggest potential directions for innovation (e.g., finding technologies with technical attributes similar to a target technology and applying distinct attributes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including intentional variability (e.g., higher sampling temperature) may increase creativity. Legal issues around AI-generated inventions (inventorship/ownership) should be considered when using AI for idea generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for claims as primary input for legal tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims contain essential features for legal novelty and patentability assessment; using claims for predictions is a sensible approach compared to titles/abstracts which are generic and do not disclose patent features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies relying on titles/abstracts may be unsuitable for automated examination tasks that require alignment with legal definitions of novelty and inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLMs potential and practical requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Large language models have shown outstanding capabilities in information extraction and may significantly improve patent IE, novelty prediction, and patentability assessment, but practical use requires labeled data, compute resources, and careful evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers are encouraged to explore powerful LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) for feature extraction and explainability, while being mindful of data, resource, and evaluation limitations; older embedding methods may be insufficient.
